strengths: The paper addresses an important practical bottleneck in video diffusion and proposes a training-free, plug-and-play caching approach.

Evaluation spans three video DiT architectures, different schedulers, resolutions, video lengths, and single- and multi-GPU configurations. The reported study of more than 1,000 videos per model and baseline is substantial.
The default configuration reports useful latency reductions while largely preserving VBench performance, including 1.61x speedup on Open-Sora and 1.90x on Latte.
The threshold and recomputation-interval ablations clearly illustrate the quality-efficiency trade-off, and the use of VBench together with LPIPS, SSIM, and PSNR provides complementary evidence.
weaknesses: The central novelty is insufficiently established. Closely related methods such as Cache Me If You Can, AdaCache, FasterCache, FORA, and SmoothCache are cited but neither compared experimentally nor carefully differentiated. In particular, the relationship to prior block caching and adaptive video-DiT caching is unclear.

Despite the “block-wise” framing, Equation 7 aggregates differences over every block into one global decision, and the text says all block features are cached or skipped together. If blocks are reused jointly, caching every intermediate block appears redundant because only the final cached output affects subsequent computation. The paper does not clearly explain what block-level granularity provides over whole-DiT/timestep caching.

The algorithm is underspecified. It is unclear precisely how decisions are made during skipped timesteps when current block features are unavailable, how caches interact with changing timestep conditioning and residual paths, and whether spatial and temporal blocks receive separate decisions. Pseudocode and a precise compute/cache schedule are needed for reproducibility.

Default baseline configurations are not consistently matched by latency or quality. For example, TeaCache is nearly twice as fast as BWCache on Open-Sora-Plan, so the broad claim that BWCache outperforms competing methods in both quality and efficiency is not supported by Table 1. Trade-off curves are provided only for Open-Sora.

The evaluation lacks human preference assessment or released videos, while static frame grids cannot establish temporal fidelity. Reproducibility details such as prompt splits, random-seed pairing, exact baseline hyperparameters, and run-to-run latency variation are also missing.

The statistical analysis is inadequately documented: Table 9 claims paired t-tests but reports confidence intervals for individual method scores rather than paired differences, omits the test statistic and effective sample size, and does not explain pairing or multiple-comparison handling.

The multi-GPU discussion conflates caching gains with hardware parallelism: the stated 17.2x speedup compares eight-GPU BWCache against the one-GPU original, whereas the same-eight-GPU algorithmic improvement is about 2.2x. This overstates the method-specific scaling benefit.

strengths: The paper addresses the practically important problem of reducing the substantial inference cost of video Diffusion Transformers.
BWCache is training-free and conceptually simple, combining feature caching, a similarity threshold, and periodic recomputation without modifying model weights.
The evaluation covers three video-generation backbones, more than 1,000 generated videos per model and baseline, several resolutions and sequence lengths, and both single- and multi-GPU settings.
The paper reports complementary efficiency and fidelity metrics and includes useful studies of the similarity threshold, reuse interval, final-step recomputation, and inference-step reduction.
weaknesses: The novelty is insufficiently established against closely related methods. The paper itself cites prior block caching, adaptive caching, and similarity-based caching approaches, including Cache Me If You Can, AdaCache, FasterCache, and SmoothCache, but does not explain precisely what substantive technical advance remains beyond averaging adjacent-feature L1 distances and applying periodic recomputation borrowed from PAB.

The method is materially underspecified. Computing the proposed indicator appears to require obtaining every block output at adjacent timesteps, whereas acceleration requires skipping those computations. The paper does not provide an algorithm or unambiguous state-transition description explaining which outputs are available during cached steps, exactly when the indicator is evaluated, and how caching is initiated and terminated.

Despite the name “block-wise caching,” Equation 7 aggregates differences over all blocks and the text appears to cache or reuse all blocks together. It is unclear whether decisions are actually made per block. This ambiguity undermines both the claimed granularity and reproducibility.

The central U-shaped redundancy observation is demonstrated using only two prompts on one model. This is inadequate evidence that the pattern generalizes across prompts, schedulers, architectures, resolutions, and motion regimes, even though generality is central to the motivation.

Several directly relevant and potentially stronger baselines cited by the paper—particularly AdaCache, FasterCache, Cache Me If You Can, and SmoothCache—are absent from the experiments. Baseline configurations and the procedure for selecting their quality-speed operating points are also not documented sufficiently.

The main comparisons are not consistently quality- or latency-matched. For example, TeaCache is substantially faster than BWCache on Open-Sora-Plan, while BWCache provides higher fidelity. A trade-off curve is shown only for Open-Sora, so the broad claim that BWCache outperforms alternatives in both quality and efficiency is not supported across models.

LPIPS, SSIM, and PSNR are computed relative to outputs from the unaccelerated model and therefore primarily measure trajectory fidelity, not absolute perceptual quality or prompt adherence. VBench helps, but there is no human evaluation, and the protocol, exact prompt composition, random-seed control, and sample count for each reported metric remain unclear.

The statistical analysis is not sufficiently rigorous or transparent. Although paired t-tests are claimed, the table reports confidence intervals for individual method means rather than paired differences, does not state the exact sample size or test assumptions, and does not address multiple comparisons. Consequently, the extremely small p-values do not independently validate the practical claims.

There are multiple reporting inconsistencies: Latte's 26.90-to-14.16-second result corresponds to about 1.90x speedup in Table 1 but is labeled 1.77x in Figure 4; Open-Sora PAB latency differs between Table 1 and Figure 4; and Table 3 omits latency despite the text citing 19.16 seconds. These errors reduce confidence in the evaluation.

Reproducibility is limited by the absence of pseudocode, model/checkpoint versions, exact baseline settings, complete prompt lists and seeds, and clear implementation details. Overall, the idea is plausible and the empirical scope is promising, but the unresolved novelty, specification, comparison, and reporting issues keep the submission below the top-tier acceptance threshold.

strengths: BWCache addresses an important practical bottleneck with a training-free, plug-and-play approach that is conceptually simple and applicable to existing video diffusion transformers.

The empirical scope is substantial: three model families, more than 1,000 generated videos per model and baseline, several resolutions and video lengths, single- and multi-GPU measurements, and multiple quality metrics.

The main operating point provides useful acceleration while largely preserving VBench quality: reported single-GPU speedups are 1.61x, 2.24x, and 1.90x on Open-Sora, Open-Sora-Plan, and Latte, respectively.
The paper includes informative threshold, reuse-interval, final-step, and reduced-sampling-step studies that expose the quality-efficiency trade-off rather than reporting only one configuration.
The block-feature analysis provides an intuitive empirical motivation for concentrating reuse in the relatively stable middle portion of the denoising trajectory.
weaknesses: The novelty over prior caching methods is limited and insufficiently isolated. The method combines a relative-feature-difference trigger resembling TeaCache-style adaptive caching with periodic recomputation adopted from PAB, while closely related block/adaptive caching work such as Cache Me If You Can and AdaCache is not evaluated experimentally.

Despite the name, the presented decision in Eq. 7 averages differences over every block and appears to trigger reuse of all blocks together. If all block outputs are reused, the computation resembles whole-denoiser or timestep-level caching; the paper does not convincingly demonstrate what distinctly block-wise behavior contributes.

The algorithm is underspecified. It is unclear how the indicator is updated during skipped timesteps when current block features have not been computed, exactly when a caching phase terminates, and how the rule reserving the last k/2 steps interacts with periodic recomputation. An explicit algorithm and complexity analysis are needed for reproducibility.

Comparisons do not consistently establish Pareto superiority at matched quality or latency. Most models are evaluated at one selected operating point; on Open-Sora-Plan, TeaCache is nearly twice as fast as BWCache, contradicting broad statements and a figure caption claiming that BWCache outperforms TeaCache in both quality and efficiency.

Several reported efficiency claims are misleading or inconsistent. The 17.2x multi-GPU figure compares eight-GPU BWCache against the one-GPU original rather than isolating caching speedup; at eight GPUs the corresponding within-hardware speedup is about 2.17x. Figure 4 also contains latency or speedup values inconsistent with Table 1.

Caching outputs for all DiT blocks may have substantial memory and bandwidth costs, especially for long high-resolution videos, but peak memory, cache size, and overhead of computing the similarity statistic are not reported.

The statistical analysis is inadequately specified: the paired observations and test construction are not described, the displayed confidence intervals appear to cover individual method means rather than paired differences, and multiple comparisons are not addressed. Extremely small p-values therefore do not by themselves validate the superiority claim.

Reproducibility details remain incomplete, including precise model versions, baseline hyperparameters and tuning protocol, prompt-set composition, random-seed control, and complete caching pseudocode. The code reference is not readable in the manuscript.

Visual evidence consists of sparse still frames, which cannot establish temporal coherence or motion preservation. VBench helps, but a human preference study or accessible video supplement would better support the perceptual-quality claims.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical bottleneck and proposes a training-free caching approach that is straightforward to integrate into pretrained video diffusion transformers.

The empirical scope is broad: five video-generation models, several caching baselines, more than 1,000 generated videos per model/baseline, multiple resolutions and sequence lengths, and both single- and multi-GPU settings.

The evaluation includes latency, VBench, reference-based fidelity metrics, memory consumption, dynamic-scene subsets, and ablations over the threshold, reuse interval, terminal recomputation, and indicator block subset.
BWCache often provides a favorable empirical quality-efficiency trade-off, including 1.61–2.60x single-GPU speedups with small reported VBench changes.
weaknesses: The central method is insufficiently specified and internally inconsistent. Equation 7 averages differences across all blocks and appears to make one global cache decision, yet the text claims that fewer individual blocks are cached when variation increases and Figure 9 reports a block reuse rate. No algorithm explains which blocks are reused, how global and per-block decisions interact, or how the indicator is evaluated during skipped steps. This makes the claimed 'block-wise' mechanism difficult to understand or reproduce.

The novelty is questionable relative to directly relevant prior work on block caching, especially Cache Me If You Can, FORA, SmoothCache, AdaCache, and related adaptive feature-reuse methods. Several are cited but not experimentally compared, and the paper does not clearly isolate what is technically new beyond using an averaged relative-L1 threshold plus periodic recomputation inherited from PAB.

There are unexplained contradictions in the ablations. The paper says that increasing the number of final non-cached steps should require more computation, but Table 9 reports decreasing latency from 1/3k to 2/3k; some quality values there also make the selected 1/2k setting appear dominated. These results cast doubt on either the definition, implementation, or reporting of a key design component.

Reproducibility is weak: the advertised code URL is blank, there is no pseudocode, exact model-specific and baseline hyperparameters are largely absent, and important details such as cache initialization, tensor reuse semantics, prompt/seed pairing, timing protocol, and threshold selection procedure are not fully documented.

The statistical analysis is not reported correctly enough to validate its claims. Table 10 gives confidence intervals for individual method means rather than paired differences, omits sample counts and test assumptions, and does not report uncertainty for latency or VBench—the metrics underlying the principal quality-efficiency claim. Small VBench differences, including scores above the original model, therefore cannot be judged for significance.

The multi-GPU headline speedups conflate caching gains with hardware scaling: for example, the stated 17.16x result compares eight-GPU BWCache against the one-GPU original, whereas the within-eight-GPU improvement is only about 2.17x. Qualitative evidence consists mainly of selected still frames and cannot adequately demonstrate preservation of temporal motion quality.

strengths: The problem is practically important: reducing the substantial inference cost of video diffusion transformers without retraining or modifying pretrained models.
The empirical study covers five video-generation architectures and reports latency, VBench, reference-similarity metrics, memory consumption, dynamic-scene results, and several ablations.
BWCache is training-free and appears to provide a useful quality-efficiency trade-off on several evaluated configurations, including up to 2.6x single-GPU speedup.
The paper recognizes relevant deployment issues such as cache-induced latent drift, final-step sensitivity, indicator overhead, and memory usage.
weaknesses: The central methodological contribution is insufficiently defined and potentially mischaracterized. Equation 7 averages differences over all blocks to produce a single timestep-level decision, while the text alternately says that all blocks are reused and that individual blocks are selectively reused. This does not clearly substantiate the claimed block-wise granularity or explain the fractional per-step block reuse rates in Figure 9.

Novelty over prior block-caching and adaptive-caching methods is weak. The method largely combines feature-distance thresholding, cached feature reuse, and periodic recomputation, while directly relevant methods such as Cache Me If You Can, AdaCache, SmoothCache, and FORA are not adequately differentiated or consistently included as baselines.

The comparisons do not establish a generally superior quality-latency frontier. Most models are evaluated at only one operating point per baseline; thresholds and reuse schedules are method-specific; and TeaCache is dramatically faster on Open-Sora-Plan. The trade-off curves in Figure 1 cover only Open-Sora, so the broad dominance claims are unsupported.

Some reported speedup claims conflate caching with multi-GPU parallelism. For example, the claimed 17.2x Open-Sora speedup compares eight-GPU BWCache against the one-GPU original; against the eight-GPU original in Table 2, the incremental speedup is only about 2.2x. The statement that BWCache has the lowest latency in almost all multi-GPU cases also overlooks TeaCache's substantially lower Open-Sora-Plan latency.

The statistical analysis is not adequately reported. Although the paper claims paired t-tests, it gives no paired-difference statistics or sample counts, and the displayed confidence intervals appear to be intervals for individual method means rather than paired effects. Their widths also appear difficult to reconcile with the claim of more than 1,000 videos for every model and baseline.

Evaluation of perceptual and temporal quality is incomplete. LPIPS, SSIM, and PSNR primarily measure similarity to the unaccelerated model rather than video quality, while VBench differences are small and no human preference study is provided. Static frame strips cannot reliably demonstrate motion preservation or temporal consistency.

There are unresolved internal inconsistencies. The last-step ablation reports lower latency as more final steps ostensibly avoid caching, contrary to the described mechanism; the notation in Equations 6 and 7 is inconsistent; and it remains unclear how the similarity indicator can be computed without performing the block computations it is intended to skip.

Reproducibility is limited: the manuscript's code-availability statement contains no usable repository link, and important implementation details—including exact per-model cache logic, baseline tuning, random-seed pairing, and statistical protocol—are missing. Overall, the promising breadth of experiments does not overcome the ambiguity in the core algorithm, weak novelty positioning, and unreliable or overstated empirical claims.

strengths: BWCache addresses an important practical bottleneck with a simple, training-free mechanism that can be integrated into pretrained video Diffusion Transformers without retraining or architectural changes.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad: five substantially different video-generation models, more than 1,000 videos per model and baseline, several caching baselines, and tests covering latency, visual fidelity, multi-GPU scaling, memory use, long/high-resolution generation, and dynamic scenes.

Results provide concrete positive evidence of competitiveness. At the quality-oriented operating point, BWCache retains VBench scores close to the original models while achieving 1.61–2.60× single-GPU speedups; it generally improves LPIPS, SSIM, and PSNR relative to PAB, TeaCache, and FasterCache.

The paper includes useful ablations of the similarity threshold, recomputation interval, protected final steps, and number of blocks used by the indicator. The comparison against simply reducing sampling steps is also informative.

The feature-variation analysis offers an intuitive motivation for adaptive reuse, and the paper documents practical costs often omitted from acceleration work, including the indicator's 10.6–22.5% latency overhead and absolute memory consumption.
weaknesses: The main methodological description is internally ambiguous. The paper calls the method block-wise and says that fewer blocks are cached when features vary more, but Equation 7 averages differences over all blocks and the surrounding text appears to make a single decision to skip or recompute all blocks. The exact cached tensor, per-block versus global decision rule, cache-update sequence, and indexing in Equation 7 must be specified algorithmically for reproducibility.

Novelty is moderate. The method largely combines an L1-based similarity threshold with feature caching, periodic recomputation adopted from PAB, and a heuristic that protects late denoising steps. Its distinction from closely related block-caching methods such as Cache Me If You Can, AdaCache, SmoothCache, and FORA is not established sharply, and several of these methods are not included as experimental baselines.

The evidence for universal quality-efficiency superiority is somewhat overstated. Baselines are mainly compared at one operating point without a documented matched-quality or matched-latency tuning protocol. TeaCache is substantially faster on Open-Sora-Plan, and full Pareto curves are shown only for Open-Sora rather than all five models.

LPIPS, SSIM, and PSNR measure agreement with the original model's particular sampled output rather than video quality itself. VBench helps, but no human preference study is provided, and qualitative evaluation consists of sparse still frames that cannot reveal temporal artifacts reliably.

Important implementation and statistical details remain incomplete: the manuscript does not clearly report prompt counts per source and model, random-seed pairing, uncertainty for latency and VBench, or sufficiently precise baseline-tuning procedures. The paired-test table reports extremely small p-values but does not clearly state the sample size and pairing unit for each test.

Memory overhead is material and occasionally approaches the capacity of an 80GB GPU. Although reduced-block indicators are studied for quality and memory, the corresponding latency and speedup effects are omitted, limiting assessment of the proposed memory-constrained variants.
